en: An overwhelming outpouring of many things at once
hook: BARRAGE: like a BARRAGE of artillery fire.
story: Barrage. An overwhelming outpouring of many things at once. The day Mitul's university results came out, he went to his grandmother's house in Cumilla for lunch. Before he could sit down, the relatives began. What was his grade? Which job would he get? Why was he so thin? When would he marry? [chuckle] Mitul smiled and kept eating through the barrage. Think of a barrage of artillery, shell after shell falling at once; a barrage of questions is just as relentless. So, what word means a flood of many things coming at you all at once? ... Barrage.

gre.s: Upon announcing the controversial policy, the minister faced a ____ of criticism so relentless that she withdrew the proposal within a week.
gre.clue: so relentless that she withdrew the proposal within a week

example: The new referee faced a barrage of whistles and jeers from the home fans after he disallowed their team's late goal.

en: Unable to produce crops, offspring, or results; empty
hook: BARREN: as empty as a BARREL with nothing inside.
story: Barren. Unable to produce crops or results; empty. After a storm surge swept salt water across the fields near Kalapara, Abul's land lay barren for two years. Nothing grew but a white crust of salt, cracking under the sun. Every morning he walked the empty field, and every morning he came back with nothing. Then the rains slowly washed the soil clean, and the first green shoots appeared. Barren is the opposite of fertile: a barren field gives nothing back. So, what word describes land too empty to grow anything? ... Barren.

gre.s: Years of intensive farming without rest had left the once fertile valley ____, its exhausted soil yielding barely enough to feed the families who tilled it.
gre.clue: its exhausted soil yielding barely enough

example: Salt water from repeated storm surges has left many coastal fields in Khulna barren, and farmers there have turned to raising crabs.

en: To be disloyal to; also, to unintentionally reveal something
bn: বিশ্বাসঘাতকতা করা; অজান্তে প্রকাশ করে ফেলা
hook: GRE trick: BETRAY often means REVEAL — your trembling hands betray your nerves.
story: Betray. To be disloyal; also, to reveal something without meaning to. At her thesis defence in Dhaka, Mahjabin answered every question in a calm, steady voice. She seemed perfectly confident. But under the table her hands were trembling, and when she reached for her glass of water, it shook so much it spilled. Her hands betrayed her nerves. The examiners smiled kindly, and she passed. On the GRE, betray often means reveal: a blush can betray embarrassment. So, what verb means to give away a hidden feeling without intending to? ... Betray.

gre.s: Although the novelist insists her characters are invented, certain details ____ an intimate knowledge of her own family's history.
gre.clue: Although the novelist insists her characters are invented

example: The card player kept a straight face, but a slight tremor in his voice betrayed his excitement about the hand he held.

en: Fake or false, though made to look real
hook: BOGUS sounds like a fake BOGEYMAN — not real.
story: Bogus. Fake or false, though made to look real. At a weekly market in Thakurgaon, a man with a loudspeaker stood on a wooden box, waving a small bottle of oil. It cured headaches, baldness, joint pain and even a broken heart, he shouted, all for just fifty taka. A small crowd gathered. Old Jobbar [chuckle] shook his head and walked on. The man's claims were completely bogus. Bogus sounds a little like bogeyman, and like a bogeyman, it is not real. So, what word describes a claim that is fake but dressed up to look real? ... Bogus.

gre.s: Investigators discovered that the clinic's impressive medical certificates were ____, printed by a shop that specialized in forgeries.
gre.clue: printed by a shop that specialized in forgeries

example: Tax officials uncovered dozens of bogus companies that existed only as names on paper and were used to move money abroad.

en: To think deeply about; to consider as a possibility
hook: CONTEMPLATE: sit in the TEMPLE and think.
story: Contemplate. To think deeply about something; also, to consider it as a possibility. When Shafiq received a job offer in Canada, he did not answer right away. That evening, he sat alone on the steps of the ghat in his hometown of Faridpur, watching the river turn gold. He contemplated his parents growing older, the friends he would miss, and the life he might build far away. Contemplate has temple inside it, from the Latin for a sacred space where priests watched the sky. So, what verb means to think long and deeply? ... Contemplate.

gre.s: Although the board had once rejected the idea outright, the company's mounting losses forced its directors at least to ____ a merger with their longtime rival.
gre.clue: mounting losses forced its directors at least to

example: Only after the third flood in five years did the family contemplate selling their land and moving to Gazipur.

en: Fake; made to imitate something genuine in order to deceive
hook: COUNTER-FEIT: made COUNTER to the real one.
story: Counterfeit. Fake; made to look like the real thing in order to deceive. Before Eid, Badal sold his best bull at a cattle market in Gabtoli. The buyer paid with a thick bundle of thousand taka notes. Something felt wrong, so Badal took the bundle to the bank booth set up at the market. The officer held a note under ultraviolet light. [gasp] Half the bundle was counterfeit. Counter means against, and feit comes from the French for made: counterfeit money is made against the real thing. So, what word describes fake money made to deceive? ... Counterfeit.

gre.s: The handbags looked convincingly authentic, but customs officials determined that they were ____, manufactured in an unlicensed workshop and stamped with a stolen logo.
gre.clue: manufactured in an unlicensed workshop and stamped with a stolen logo

example: Pharmacists warn that counterfeit medicines, which look identical to the real ones, may contain nothing but chalk and sugar.

en: Seeming difficult or intimidating enough to discourage you
hook: DAUNTING sounds like 'DON'T even try', which is what the task seems to say.
story: Daunting. So difficult that it seems discouraging. On her first night of GRE preparation, Raisa opened a list of three thousand words. She scrolled and scrolled, and the list never seemed to end. [sigh] It felt daunting, almost impossible. Then her tutor showed her how to learn just thirty words a day, with a story for each one. One small set at a time, the mountain became a staircase. The opposite is undaunted, meaning not discouraged at all. So, what word describes a task so big that it seems to say: do not even try? ... Daunting.

gre.s: Though the task of cataloguing ten thousand manuscripts seemed ____ at first, the archivists found it manageable once they divided the work.
gre.clue: found it manageable once they divided the work

example: Swimming across the Bosphorus seemed daunting to Rehana, but she trained for a year and finished the race in under two hours.

en: Careful in what one says or does, to avoid causing offense or revealing secrets
hook: DISCREET keeps secrets; DISCRETE means separate. Two E's together are 'discreet' — they keep each other's secrets.
story: Discreet. Careful about what you say or do, to avoid offence or keep secrets. When Shila's father lost his job, the family had no money for her school fees. Her neighbour, Aunt Rokhsana, heard about it. She did not tell anyone in the lane. Instead, she quietly paid the fees and slipped the receipt to Shila's mother in a folded newspaper. Nobody else ever knew. She was always discreet. Discreet keeps secrets; discrete means separate. In discreet, the two e's sit together, keeping each other's secret. So, what word describes someone careful to keep things private? ... Discreet.

gre.s: The ambassador was chosen for the delicate mission because she was famously ____, never revealing confidential information even to close friends.
gre.clue: never revealing confidential information even to close friends

example: The hotel staff are famously discreet, so film stars can stay there for weeks without their visit appearing in the papers.

en: Inactive for now, as if asleep, but able to wake later
hook: DORMANT: sleeping in a DORM.
story: Dormant. Inactive for now, as if asleep, but able to wake later. Tuli's grandmother had been a fine singer as a young bride, but she stopped singing when life grew busy. For forty years her voice stayed silent. Then, at Tuli's wedding, the women began a folk song and forgot the second verse. Grandmother quietly sang it, clear and strong. [gasp] Her talent had only been dormant. Dormant comes from the Latin for sleep, as in dormitory, the room where students sleep. So, what word describes something sleeping now, but able to wake again? ... Dormant.

gre.s: Scientists warned that the volcano, though ____ for nearly two centuries, had begun showing signs of renewed activity and could erupt within months.
gre.clue: had begun showing signs of renewed activity

example: The chickenpox virus can lie dormant in nerve cells for decades before returning as shingles later in life.

en: To imitate someone you admire in order to match or surpass them
hook: EMULATE: your hero's EMblem; you copy them to become as good.
story: Emulate. To imitate someone you admire, hoping to equal or surpass them. When Joba's cousin became the first doctor from their village in Jhalokathi, the whole village came out to greet her. Joba was twelve. From that day she tried to emulate her cousin in every way: she woke early to study, and kept neat notes. Ten years later, Joba entered medical college too. Emulate means more than copy; it carries a sense of friendly rivalry, aiming to match your hero. So, what verb means to copy someone you admire, hoping to match them? ... Emulate.

gre.s: Many young composers sought to ____ the master's style, hoping that by imitating his methods they might one day equal his achievements.
gre.clue: hoping that by imitating his methods they might one day equal

example: Hoping to emulate South Korea's rapid rise, the government poured money into technical schools and electronics factories.

en: To get out of or dodge something by being clever or sly
hook: EVADE: like an EVASIVE dodge.
story: Evade. To escape or dodge something, often cleverly. Every Friday, Ilma's family tries to give their cat Mishti a bath. Every Friday, she evades them. She slips under the bed, squeezes behind the fridge, and once climbed onto the top of the cupboard. [laugh] This week, three people chased her for half an hour, [sigh] and she still evaded every hand. Evade comes from the Latin for going out: e means out, so to evade is to slip out of reach. So, what verb means to cleverly dodge or escape something? ... Evade.

gre.s: The fugitive managed to ____ capture for nearly a decade by moving constantly and using a series of false identities.
gre.clue: by moving constantly and using a series of false identities

example: The fox evaded the hunting dogs by doubling back through a shallow stream, where they lost its scent.

en: Spending too much money; excessive and beyond what is reasonable
hook: EXTRA-VAGANT: goes EXTRA far beyond limits.
story: Extravagant. Spending far too much; excessive and beyond what is sensible. With his very first salary, Rubayet bought the newest phone on the market, paying almost three months' wages in instalments. He showed it proudly to his mother in Sirajganj. She held it, quiet for a moment, then thought of the leaking roof at home. "Very beautiful," she said softly. Rubayet suddenly felt how extravagant it was. Extra means beyond, and vagant comes from the Latin for wandering, as in vagabond: extravagant spending wanders far beyond the limits. So, what word describes spending that goes far too far? ... Extravagant.

gre.s: Critics condemned the mayor's ____ renovation of his office, which included marble floors and gold fixtures, at a time of severe budget cuts.
gre.clue: marble floors and gold fixtures

example: The club's extravagant spending on foreign players left it unable to pay its groundskeepers by the end of the season.

en: Incapable of producing any useful result; pointless
hook: FUTILE: no FUTURE in it.
story: Futile. Producing no useful result; pointless. Caught in a sudden Dhaka downpour, Rimi sat in a rickshaw with a thin plastic sheet held over her knees. She pulled it up to her chin, and the rain soaked her back. She tucked it behind her, and the rain soaked her feet. Within minutes she was wet from head to toe. She [laugh] gave up and let the rain fall. Every effort had been futile. Futile comes from the Latin for leaky: like pouring water into a leaking pot. So, what word describes an effort that achieves nothing? ... Futile.

gre.s: Realizing that further resistance would be ____, the outnumbered garrison surrendered without firing another shot.
gre.clue: the outnumbered garrison surrendered

example: Bailing water out of the leaking boat was futile, so the fishermen rowed hard for the nearest sandbank instead.

en: To create difficulties that slow or delay something
hook: HINDER: holds you BEHIND.
story: Hinder. To create difficulties that slow something down. On the morning of her final exam, Shapla stepped out of her house in Narayanganj to find the road under knee-deep water. No rickshaw would come. The flood hindered her at every step, but she tied up her dress, held her bag over her head, and waded for twenty minutes. She reached the hall just in time. The water could hinder her, but not stop her. Hinder shares its root with hind and behind: what hinders you holds you back. So, what verb means to slow someone down with obstacles? ... Hinder.

gre.s: Bureaucratic delays continue to ____ the delivery of aid, leaving thousands of flood victims without food.
gre.clue: leaving thousands of flood victims without food

example: Thick smoke from the burning warehouse hindered the firefighters, who could barely see the hoses in their own hands.

en: A person who claims beliefs or virtues they don't follow
hook: HYPOCRITE: a Greek actor (hypokrites), playing a role.
story: Hypocrite. A person who claims beliefs or virtues they do not practise. At every family dinner in Sylhet, Uncle Mosharraf gives the children a long speech about phones. No screens at the table, he says; talk to each other. One evening, little Rohan noticed his uncle's phone glowing under the tablecloth, and he was watching cricket. Everyone saw it. Uncle Mosharraf blushed and admitted he was a hypocrite. Hypocrite comes from the Greek word for an actor on a stage, playing a role. So, what do you call someone who preaches what they do not practise? ... Hypocrite.

gre.s: The minister who lectured citizens about saving electricity was exposed as a ____ when reporters discovered that his own residence ran air conditioners day and night.
gre.clue: his own residence ran air conditioners day and night

example: Ruma called her brother a hypocrite for nagging her about screen time while he scrolled through his phone at every meal.

en: Lasting for an unknown length of time; not clearly defined
hook: IN-DEFINITE: NOT DEFINED.
story: Indefinite. Lasting for an unknown length of time; not clearly defined. One morning, a notice went up at Ratul's university in Chattogram: all classes were suspended for an indefinite period. No date for reopening, no reason given. Students packed their bags and went home, unsure whether to study, find a job or simply wait. For Ratul, the indefinite break felt like a pause button nobody would press again. Indefinite means not definite: no fixed end, no clear limit. So, what word describes a period with no fixed end? ... Indefinite.

gre.s: The strike was declared to be ____: union leaders refused to set any end date and vowed to continue until every one of their demands had been met.
gre.clue: refused to set any end date

example: After the knee injury, the striker was ruled out for an indefinite period, and the club began searching for a replacement.

en: Starting and stopping at irregular times rather than continuing steadily
hook: INTER-MITTENT: stopping and starting, with gaps IN BETWEEN.
story: Intermittent. Starting and stopping at irregular times. Anisa was in the middle of an online interview with a university abroad when her internet began to fail. The screen froze, then came back, then froze again. The professor's voice arrived in pieces. Anisa kept smiling, repeating her answers patiently, while her brother ran to restart the router. The connection stayed intermittent all hour, but she got the offer. Inter means between, and the word means leaving gaps in between. So, what word describes something that keeps stopping and starting? ... Intermittent.

gre.s: Electricity in the village was ____ at best, flickering on for an hour or so and then vanishing for the rest of the evening.
gre.clue: flickering on for an hour or so and then vanishing

example: The lighthouse gives out an intermittent flash, so sailors can tell it apart from the steady lights of the town behind it.

en: Rich, elaborate, and generous; to give generously
hook: LAVISH: like a LAVA flow of luxury.
story: Lavish. Rich and generous; as a verb, to give generously. When her grandchildren visit her in Barishal for Eid, Nanu lavishes food on them from morning to night. There is beef curry, three kinds of fish, pulao, sweet yogurt, and fresh pitha every afternoon. The children beg her to stop. [laugh] She only fills their plates again. It is a lavish welcome, every single year. Lavish comes from an old French word for a downpour of rain: lavish generosity pours down like rain. So, what word describes a welcome that is rich and generous? ... Lavish.

gre.s: Critics accused the company of hypocrisy: even as it cut workers' wages, it held a ____ banquet for its executives, complete with imported wine and live music.
gre.clue: complete with imported wine and live music

example: For the school's hundredth anniversary, former students paid for a lavish dinner in the courtyard, with musicians brought from Kolkata.

en: Everyday and ordinary, with nothing exciting about it
hook: MUNDANE: MONDAY-ish, ordinary routine.
story: Mundane. Ordinary and everyday, with nothing exciting about it. Every day, Habib wakes at six, takes the same bus to his office in Motijheel, files the same papers, and comes home at seven. When his daughter asked what he did at work, he said it was all mundane. Then she showed him her school diary: every evening, she had written how happy she felt when he came home. His mundane life meant everything to her. Mundane comes from the Latin mundus, world: mundane things belong to the everyday world. So, what word describes life that is ordinary and routine? ... Mundane.

gre.s: The novelist has a gift for transforming ____ events, such as a trip to the grocery store, into moments of startling beauty.
gre.clue: such as a trip to the grocery store

example: The poet's notebooks are full of mundane lists, such as eggs, lamp oil and stamps, scribbled between drafts of famous poems.

en: Suggesting that something bad is going to happen
hook: OMINOUS: an OMEN of bad things.
story: Ominous. Suggesting that something bad is about to happen. Crossing the old bamboo bridge over the canal near his school in Pirojpur, Jibon heard a long, low creak beneath his feet. Then another, louder. The whole bridge swayed slightly. The sound was ominous. He hurried back to the bank and warned the other children to go around by the road. Two days later, the middle of the bridge collapsed. Ominous comes from omen, a sign of what is to come. So, what word describes a sound or sign that warns of trouble ahead? ... Ominous.

gre.s: The doctors' sudden silence and averted eyes were ____, and the family braced themselves for bad news before a single word was spoken.
gre.clue: braced themselves for bad news

example: An ominous creak came from the old wooden bridge as the loaded truck rolled slowly onto it.

en: Causing a strong reaction, especially anger or interest; deliberately stimulating
hook: PROVOCATIVE: it PROVOKES you.
story: Provocative. Causing a strong reaction, especially anger or deep interest. The topic at the university debate in Sylhet was, "Exams kill learning." Half the audience murmured angrily before anyone had spoken. Teachers frowned. Students leaned forward. By the end, the hall was arguing loudly, and the discussion went on for hours in the canteen. The topic was deliberately provocative. Provocative comes from provoke, to call forth a reaction. So, what word describes something designed to stir strong feelings? ... Provocative.

gre.s: The museum's ____ exhibit, featuring images designed to shock, drew both furious protests and record crowds.
gre.clue: featuring images designed to shock

example: The columnist's provocative claim that cricket was ruining Bangladeshi schools drew thousands of angry letters in a single week.

en: Acting with care and thought for the future; wise and careful
hook: PRUDENT: a PRUDE about risk; careful, never wild.
story: Prudent. Careful, sensible and thinking about the future. For years, Kaberi's mother set aside a small part of every salary in a savings account. Her husband teased her, saying she should enjoy the money now. Then the factory where he worked closed, and he was without a job for eight months. Those savings paid for rent, food and school fees until he found new work. Her husband never teased her again. She had been prudent. Prudent is a shortened form of provident: seeing ahead and providing for it. So, what word describes someone wise and careful about the future? ... Prudent.

gre.s: Given the volatile market, analysts considered it ____ to diversify investments rather than stake everything on a single stock.
gre.clue: rather than stake everything on a single stock

example: Before the long hike, the students thought it prudent to leave a copy of their route with the forest office at Lawachara.

en: The complete set of skills, songs, or works someone can perform
hook: REPERTOIRE: the REPORT of everything you can perform.
story: Repertoire. The full set of songs, skills or works that someone can perform. On the slow train from Dhaka to Mohanganj, a blind singer named Kashem walks from coach to coach with his ektara. Passengers call out requests: Lalon, Hason Raja, old film songs, even new ones from the radio. He seems to know them all, hundreds of songs held in memory. His repertoire never runs dry. Repertoire comes from the Latin for an inventory, a full list of everything stored. So, what word means the complete range of songs or skills someone can perform? ... Repertoire.

gre.s: Although the pianist was celebrated mainly for her Chopin, her ____ was surprisingly broad, extending from medieval dances to experimental contemporary works.
gre.clue: extending from medieval dances to experimental contemporary works

example: By her third season, the young spin bowler had added a quicker ball and a googly to her repertoire.

en: To give official approval to; also, a penalty for breaking a rule
hook: SANCTION has two opposite meanings: APPROVAL and PUNISHMENT. Watch the context!
story: Sanction. To give official approval; also, a penalty for breaking a rule. The school committee in Feni finally sanctioned the class ten picnic to Cox's Bazar. The students [laugh] cheered so loudly the headmaster had to cover his ears. Then he announced the rules: anyone caught littering on the beach would face sanctions, including a week of cleaning the school grounds. Sanction has two opposite meanings: approval, and punishment. Watch the context. So, what word can mean both official permission and a penalty? ... Sanction.

gre.s: Although the council refused to formally ____ the festival, it took no action to stop the residents from holding it.
gre.clue: it took no action to stop the residents

example: The cricket board refused to sanction the tour, so the players travelled to the tournament as private individuals.

en: Angry, often violent quarrelling between people or groups
hook: STRIFE: STRIKES and FIGHTS.
story: Strife. Angry, bitter quarrelling between people or groups. After their father died, three brothers in Chuadanga fought over his land for years. They took each other to court, stopped attending each other's weddings, and their children grew up as strangers. The strife spread to wives, cousins, and even neighbours. At last their elderly mother gathered them in the courtyard and said she would not live to see it continue. The strife ended that day. Strife is related to strive: both involve struggle. So, what word means bitter conflict between people? ... Strife.

gre.s: Years of ethnic ____ had left the region impoverished, its villages divided and its farms abandoned.
gre.clue: its villages divided and its farms abandoned

example: Years of family strife over the inheritance ended only when the eldest sister sold the house and divided the money equally.

en: Strict, precise, and exacting
hook: STRINGENT: tied up with tight STRINGS.
story: Stringent. Strict, precise and demanding. At the export garment factory where Selina works in Ashulia, every shirt passes through stringent checks. Inspectors measure each seam with a ruler, count stitches per inch, and pull on every button. One loose thread, and the shirt goes back. Selina once found the rules too stringent, but now she is proud that her shirts sell in shops around the world. Stringent shares a Latin root with strict and constrict, meaning to draw tight. So, what word describes rules that are strict and exacting? ... Stringent.

gre.s: Because the drug's side effects were potentially severe, regulators imposed ____ testing requirements before approving it.
gre.clue: potentially severe

example: Garment factories in Gazipur must now meet stringent fire safety rules, including sprinklers and at least two exits on every floor.

en: Seeming to turn up everywhere at once
hook: UBIQUITOUS: 'you BE QUITE everywhere'.
story: Ubiquitous. Seeming to be everywhere at once. Wherever you go in Bangladesh, you find a tea stall. On city corners and village crossroads, beside ferry ghats and hospital gates, at bus stops and university gates, someone is pouring milky tea into small glass cups. Arnob's friend from Japan said he had never seen anything so ubiquitous. Ubiquitous comes from the Latin ubique, meaning everywhere. So, what word describes something you find everywhere you look? ... Ubiquitous.

gre.s: Once a luxury owned by a privileged few, the mobile phone has become so ____ that even remote villages now rely on it for banking.
gre.clue: Once a luxury owned by a privileged few

example: Plastic is now so ubiquitous that scientists have found tiny fragments of it in Arctic snow and even in human blood.

en: Thinking about the future with imagination and wisdom
hook: VISIONARY: has a VISION of the future.
story: Visionary. Thinking about the future with imagination and wisdom. Thirty years ago, on a remote char in the Brahmaputra, Hosneara started a school for girls on a boat. Parents laughed, saying girls would only marry young anyway. She ignored them. The boat sailed from village to village, carrying books and a teacher. Today, many of her students are teachers and nurses. Everyone now calls her a visionary. Visionary comes from vision: a visionary sees a future others cannot yet imagine. So, what word describes someone who imagines a better future and builds it? ... Visionary.

gre.s: Dismissed in her own time as a dreamer, the urban planner is now hailed as a ____ whose ideas anticipated modern sustainable cities.
gre.clue: whose ideas anticipated modern sustainable cities

example: Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain was a visionary who imagined, in 1905, a land where women ran the country and men stayed at home.

en: Lively energy and strength of body or spirit
hook: VITALITY: VITAL life energy.
story: Vitality. Lively energy and strength of body or spirit. Every morning at six, a seventy-year-old woman named Feroza leads a walking group around Ramna Park. She walks faster than people half her age, cracks jokes, and scolds anyone who falls behind. [laugh] Younger members try to keep up, panting. Her vitality inspires the whole group. Vitality comes from the Latin vita, life, as in vital and vitamin: vitality is life energy itself. So, what word means lively energy and spirit? ... Vitality.

gre.s: Even at eighty, the sculptor retained a remarkable ____, working twelve hours a day and climbing scaffolding that exhausted assistants half her age.
gre.clue: working twelve hours a day

example: Street vendors, buskers and late-night tea stalls give the old quarter a vitality that the new shopping malls cannot match.

en: Justified; having good reason
hook: WARRANTED: a WARRANT gives justification.
story: Warranted. Justified; having good reason. When Mithila's mother made her carry a raincoat on a sunny day in Sylhet, Mithila rolled her eyes all the way to the bus stop. By afternoon, black clouds rolled in and heavy rain hammered the city. Mithila pulled out the raincoat, dry and grateful. Her mother's caution had been warranted. A warrant is an official document that gives authority; warranted means backed by good reason. Unwarranted means without reason. So, what word describes worry or action that is justified? ... Warranted.

gre.s: Given the company's long record of concealing defects, the regulators' skepticism about its latest safety claims seems entirely ____.
gre.clue: Given the company's long record of concealing defects

example: The coach's anger was warranted, since three players had skipped training to attend a party the night before the final.
